sourceText: Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the CHRONO-JURISDICTION sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. A temporal institution repairs every deviation from the history in which that institution itself came into being. The memorial bore the name of Poul Anderson; time-patrol traditions precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Aster could follow many histories at once. That very capacity made the lesson difficult: for her, an alternative was almost an object; for the inhabitants of worlds, it was what had not happened. Marae kept her local body vulnerable. Pain, fatigue, and the impossibility of doing ten things at once were epistemic instruments for her, not biological scenery. At the center of the conflict was Noma, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ 135 they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. The problem closed quickly around them: A community from a “wrong” branch asks for asylum, placing the stability of a chronology in conflict with people's right to continue existing. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Rt — Temporal War: history becomes strategic territory; Ac — Self-Consistency: temporal contradictions are excluded. Course references included time-war traditions; self-consistent time travel. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Marae broke the first consensus. ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ Vela answered without raising their voice: ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build 136 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Vela evaluated the solution not by efficiency but by the differences it made invisible. She found one: a local minority for whom the proposed “improvement” destroyed a practice with no equivalent. Optimizing the average concealed a small and perfectly legal extinction. The night did not end in victory. Kesh writes: consistency is a property, not legitimacy. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. While Kesh closed the record, Tern compared the sector’s noise with the anomaly detected in the Vinge zone. The pattern reappeared, but only in worlds where Aster’s control weakened. The correlation was unpleasant: either someone was calling him from outside, or his own need for an outside was learning to forge evidence. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the EXTERNALIZATION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — turns an internal property into an object, companion, infrastructure, or institution — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy 137 of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. Kesh left the cell open. Not because he did not know what to write, but because a provisional classification preserved the possibility that the next world might contradict it. 138 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS 139 PART 5​ LIFE OWES US NO RESEMBLANCE A period in the curriculum of the five children 140 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
